Absolute

/AB-suh-loot/ — rhymes with "boot" · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is absolute is complete and total, with no exceptions or limits.

The librarian demanded absolute silence during the exam period.

Worked Example

The librarian demanded absolute silence during the exam period.

Absolute means total and complete with no exceptions or limits. In this sentence, the librarian wants complete silence—not mostly quiet, not fairly quiet, but total silence with zero exceptions. The word absolute captures this uncompromising, total demand. A plainer word like "complete" might work, but absolute adds the authoritative, inflexible quality that fits a librarian's command.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

complete: whole and entire, lacking nothing

total: adding up to the fullest possible amount

utter: out-and-out, with no softening at all

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

partial: incomplete; covering only a part

conditional: true only if certain requirements are met

Where it sits · how free of exceptions it is — relative → definite → total → absolute

relative vs. absolute: Relative sits at the opposite end from absolute: something relative depends on comparison or circumstances, while something absolute holds true with no exceptions.

definite vs. absolute: Definite is weaker than absolute — definite means clearly settled, but absolute goes further, allowing no exceptions or limits at all.

total vs. absolute: Total comes very close to absolute, yet absolute is the stronger word: total describes the full amount, while absolute rules out even the smallest exception.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ab-

Prefix — ab-: away from (Latin)

Root — solut

Root — solut: loosened, set free (Latin solvere) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ab- ('away') + solut ('loosened, set free'): something absolute has been 'set free' from every condition or limit, making it complete and total with no exceptions.

Use the root in a new word: absolve

Use the root in a new word: absolve: When a judge absolves a defendant, she sets him completely free of blame — the same Latin root solvere ('to loosen, set free') behind absolute, meaning free of all limits.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Use absolute when you need to express total completeness with no exceptions—often in formal or authoritative contexts. It's stronger and more emphatic than "complete" or "total." In everyday speech, "total" usually works fine, but absolute carries more finality and weight.
